narrative: The model estimated a 91.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because your law school application was tied to that prediction, it was rejected; this does not mean you cannot succeed, but it means the evidence submitted looked strongly consistent with first-try bar failure. The strongest driver was your third-year class standing: being in the lowest decile placed you far below accepted students, whose average was around the sixth decile, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the second-strongest factor; also being in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, reinforced that risk. Your LSAT score of 37 was the third-most influential factor, but it worked in your favor: it is close to the accepted-student average of about 37, so it slightly pushed toward passing rather than failure. The rejection therefore rests mainly on very low first- and third-year class ranks, not on gender or race. Next, ask admissions for specific feedback, meet with academic advisors about why your class standing was low, and build a concrete plan to strengthen your academic record before reapplying. You may also consider retaking the LSAT if practice results suggest a higher score, and document any circumstances affecting your earlier performance.
